title: Ship Fire Jolts Strait of Hormuz as US-Iran Attacks Widen to Kuwait, Bahrain and Jordan
excerpt: A vessel burns near Oman as the US conducts its ninth straight night of strikes on Iran and Tehran hits Gulf state infrastructure, sending Brent crude above $90 a barrel.
body:
• A vessel caught fire near Oman's Kumzar in the Strait of Hormuz as the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency warned ships to transit with caution, though the cause remains unconfirmed.
  • The US conducted a ninth straight night of strikes against Iran while Tehran hit targets in Kuwait and Bahrain, including a desalination plant and an AI centre.
  • Brent crude surpassed $90 a barrel on Monday — its highest since June — after gaining nearly 16% last week as shipping through the strait slowed to a trickle.
  • Only four vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, down from eight the previous day, with both the US naval blockade and Iran's closure of the waterway choking global oil flows.

A vessel on fire near the Strait of Hormuz, a desalination plant hit in Kuwait, and Iranian missiles striking Bahrain — the US-Iran conflict widened sharply over the weekend as both sides tested the limits of escalation and the world's most important oil chokepoint edged closer to full shutdown.

Fire in the Strait

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported early Monday that a vessel was on fire approximately eight nautical miles northwest of Kumzar, Oman, within the Strait of Hormuz. "Vessels are advised to transit with caution and report any suspicious activity to UKMTO while authorities investigate," the agency said. The cause of the fire has not been confirmed.

The incident comes days after Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed two oil tankers exploded and caught fire after passing through what Tehran described as a mined route south of the strait. The US Central Command rejected those claims, saying the reported tanker explosions "did not occur as described."

What is not in dispute is that shipping through the strait has collapsed. Only four vessels made the transit on Sunday, down from eight the previous day, according to LSEG data. The strait normally handles one-fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas shipments.

The War Widens Beyond Iran

The weekend's most alarming development was the expansion of the conflict's geographic footprint. Iran announced attacks on Gulf countries hosting US airbases, including Bahrain, Qatar, and Kuwait. The Revolutionary Guards said they destroyed Bahrain's main artificial intelligence centre with ballistic missiles and drones and attacked a US drone depot there.

"If U.S. strikes continue for several more days, we will move into a phase of full-scale offensive operations."

— Mohsen Rezaei, adviser to Iran's supreme leader and former IRGC commander

In Kuwait, an Iranian strike hit a power generation and water desalination station, causing a fire and disrupting electricity generation units. The rich Arab Gulf states depend on such plants to make their desert cities habitable — when Iran struck a Kuwaiti desalination plant on March 30, it was regarded as a major escalation.

The US, meanwhile, struck bridges, an airport, and a train station in southern Iran, marking the first time it described targets as "military logistics infrastructure." Central Command said it completed a ninth consecutive night of strikes targeting Iranian military coastal surveillance, air defense facilities, and missile storage sites.

Rising Cost in Lives and Oil

Three more US service members were confirmed killed over the weekend — two in Jordan from Iranian ballistic missile and drone attacks, and one in northern Iraq during the detonation of an unexploded Iranian drone. The total US death toll in the conflict now stands at 17, with over 50,000 uniformed personnel deployed across the Middle East.

Iran's Health Ministry reported 50 people killed and more than 500 wounded in US strikes over the past three weeks.

Oil markets responded with alarm. Brent crude climbed 3% to $90.79 a barrel on Monday, its highest since June 11, extending a 15.9% weekly gain — the biggest since April. "Oil markets are still too complacent about the potential fallout for inventories, which are at the tightest of the past five years," Barclays analyst Amarpreet Singh warned.

What It Means for India and the Diaspora

India imports roughly 85% of its crude oil, and the Strait of Hormuz remains a critical supply artery. With both a US naval blockade and Iran's closure squeezing the waterway, every dollar added to the barrel lands directly on India's current account deficit and consumer fuel bills. India has already hiked diesel and jet fuel export taxes in response.

For the estimated 8.9 million Indians living in Gulf Cooperation Council countries, the situation is increasingly unsettling. India has urged citizens to postpone travel to Iran, and the State Department has issued a worldwide caution alert warning Americans, including Indian-Americans, of heightened risk. Gulf airspace closures have disrupted flights, and Kuwait's infrastructure damage underscores that the conflict's fallout is no longer confined to Iranian and US military assets.
